problems.title: Sari-Sari Budget
problems.statement:
### A1 - Sari-Sari Budget

Totoy has a fixed budget at Aling Nena's sari-sari store, and he wants to buy as many DIFFERENT items as he can (one piece of each item, he is not greedy for duplicates, just for quantity).

Given his budget and the price of every item in the store, what is the largest number of items he can buy?

## Algorithm Corner
A greedy algorithm repeatedly makes the choice that looks best right now, and never looks back. It only works when you can argue that the locally-best choice never hurts.

Here: if Totoy buys some set of items, swapping any item for a cheaper one he has not bought can only lower the total. So the best plan is always 'buy the cheapest items first'. Sorting the prices turns 'cheapest first' into a simple left-to-right loop.

## Hint
Sort the prices. Walk through them from cheapest to priciest, keeping a running total, and stop as soon as the next item would break the budget.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `max_items`. It has two parameters:
- `budget`, an int.
- `prices`, a list of `n` ints, the price of each item.

It must return an int: the maximum number of items that can be bought with total price at most `budget`.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: max_items(50, [20, 5, 30, 10, 8]) => 4
Example 2: max_items(3, [4, 5]) => 0
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 15,000
- 1 <= each price <= 10^6
- 0 <= budget <= 10^11

## Scoring
- You get 30 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 12.
- You get 50 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 1,500.
- You get 80 points if you solve all test cases.
- Your score is the best tier you fully solve.

problems.title: AVR Booking Frenzy
problems.statement:
### A2 - AVR Booking Frenzy

The Audio-Visual Room (AVR) is the most contested room on campus. Many orgs filed a request, each for a time slot [start, end]: the org needs the AVR from `start` until `end`.

Two events can both be held if they do not overlap. If one ends at exactly the moment the other starts, that is fine. The AVR manager wants to approve as many events as possible. What is that maximum?

## Algorithm Corner
Activity selection is the classic greedy-by-sorting problem. Which sort key? Not the start time (a very long event can start first and block everything). Not the length (a short event in the middle can split two good ones).

Sort by END time. The event that finishes earliest leaves the most room for everything after it, so you can always safely take it, then take the next event that starts at or after it ends, and so on.

## Hint
Sort by end time. Keep the end time of the last event you accepted. Accept an event if its start is at least that end time.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `max_events`. Its only parameter is `events`, a list of `n` pairs `[start, end]` of ints with `start < end`.

It must return an int: the maximum number of events that can be held with no two overlapping.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: max_events([[1, 4], [3, 5], [0, 6], [5, 7], [3, 9], [5, 9], [6, 10], [8, 11]]) => 3
Example 2: max_events([[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]]) => 3
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 15,000
- 0 <= start < end <= 2 * 10^6

## Scoring
- You get 30 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 10.
- You get 50 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 1,500.
- You get 100 points if you solve all test cases.
- Your score is the best tier you fully solve.

problems.title: Barkada Meetup
problems.statement:
### A3 - Barkada Meetup

A barkada lives along Katipunan Avenue, which we model as a number line. Friend i lives at position `positions[i]`. They want to meet at a single spot (any integer position) so that the TOTAL distance everyone has to walk is as small as possible.

What is that minimum total walking distance?

## Algorithm Corner
This is a famous fact: on a number line, the point that minimises the total distance to a set of points is the MEDIAN. Moving the meeting spot one step right helps everyone on the right and hurts everyone on the left, so you stop moving when the two sides are balanced. Sort, and look at the middle element.

## Hint
Try a tiny case by hand: positions 1, 2, 10. Where is the best meeting spot? Now add a friend at 50 and see how it changes. Sorting the positions makes the answer easy to see.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `meeting_point`. Its only parameter is `positions`, a non-empty list of `n` ints.

It must return an int: the minimum over all integer meeting spots `t` of the sum of `|positions[i] - t|`.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: meeting_point([1, 2, 10]) => 9
Example 2: meeting_point([4, 8]) => 4
```

## Constraints
- 1 <= n <= 15,000
- -10^10 <= positions[i] <= 10^10

## Scoring
- You get 30 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 10 and |positions[i]| <= 30.
- You get 50 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 1,500.
- You get 120 points if you solve all test cases.

problems.title: Fiesta Donations
problems.statement:
### B1 - Fiesta Donations

The barangay fiesta lasted `n` days. The treasurer wrote down the net donations of each day (a day can be negative if the expenses were bigger than the donations).

Now the barangay captain keeps asking questions like: 'What was the total from day 3 to day 8?' The treasurer is tired of re-adding the same numbers again and again. Can you answer all the questions fast?

## Algorithm Corner
Prefix sums: build an array `pre` where `pre[k]` is the sum of the first `k` values (so `pre[0] = 0`). Then the sum of days l..r (1-indexed) is simply `pre[r] - pre[l-1]`, answered in O(1) after O(n) preparation.

values = 5 2 7 1    pre = 0 5 7 14 15
sum of days 2..4 = pre[4] - pre[1] = 15 - 5 = 10

Whenever you see MANY 'sum of a range' questions, think prefix sums.

## Hint
Do not loop over l..r for every query. Compute `pre` once, then every query is one subtraction.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `range_sums`. It has two parameters:
- `values`, a list of `n` ints (day 1 is `values[0]`).
- `queries`, a list of `q` pairs `[l, r]` with `1 <= l <= r <= n` (1-indexed, inclusive).

It must return a list of `q` ints: for each query, the sum of days `l` to `r`, in order.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: range_sums([5, 2, 7, 1], [[1, 4], [2, 4], [3, 3]]) => [15, 10, 7]
```

## Constraints
- 1 <= n <= 15,000
- 0 <= q <= 15,000
- |values[i]| <= 10^6

## Scoring
- You get 30 points if you solve all test cases where n, q <= 10.
- You get 50 points if you solve all test cases where n, q <= 1,500.
- You get 80 points if you solve all test cases.
- Your score is the best tier you fully solve.

problems.title: Christmas Lights
problems.statement:
### B2 - Christmas Lights

Come December, the Quezon Memorial Circle is lined with `n` light bulbs in a row, all starting at brightness 0. The electrician flips a long series of switches. Each switch affects a stretch of bulbs: it ADDS some value `v` to the brightness of every bulb from position `l` to position `r` (the value can be negative, which dims them).

After all the switches, what is the brightness of each bulb?

## Algorithm Corner
Difference arrays are 'prefix sums in reverse'. Instead of touching every bulb in l..r, you mark only the two endpoints: add `v` at index `l` and subtract `v` at index `r+1`. Later, a running sum over the marks rebuilds the real values, because the +v keeps 'switching on' for every bulb to its right until the -v cancels it.

n = 5, add 3 to bulbs 1..3:   marks = 0 3 0 0 -3 0   running sum = 0 3 3 3 0

## Hint
Make an array `marks` of size n+1. For each operation do exactly two updates. At the end, walk left to right with a running total.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `final_brightness`. It has two parameters:
- `n`, the number of bulbs (positions are 0-indexed: `0` to `n-1`).
- `operations`, a list of triples `[l, r, v]` with `0 <= l <= r < n` meaning: add `v` to every bulb from `l` to `r`, inclusive.

It must return a list of `n` ints: the final brightness of each bulb.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: final_brightness(5, [[1, 3, 3], [0, 4, 1]]) => [1, 4, 4, 4, 1]
Example 2: final_brightness(3, []) => [0, 0, 0]
```

## Constraints
- 1 <= n <= 15,000
- 0 <= q <= 15,000
- |v| <= 1,000

## Scoring
- You get 30 points if you solve all test cases where n, q <= 10.
- You get 50 points if you solve all test cases where n, q <= 1,500.
- You get 100 points if you solve all test cases.
- Your score is the best tier you fully solve.

problems.title: Ipon Challenge
problems.statement:
### B3 - Ipon Challenge

You joined the Ipon Challenge! Every day you write down how much your savings changed (negative if you spent more than you saved that day, zero if nothing changed).

A 'streak' is any stretch of one or more consecutive days. You want to know how many different streaks have a total change of EXACTLY `target` pesos. Two streaks are different if they start or end on different days, even if they contain the same numbers.

## Algorithm Corner
Combine prefix sums with a dictionary. Let `pre[j]` be the running total after day j. The streak from day i+1 to day j has total `pre[j] - pre[i]`. It equals `target` exactly when `pre[i] = pre[j] - target`.

So while sweeping left to right, keep a dict that counts how many times each prefix value has appeared so far. At every day, the number of streaks ENDING today is `count[pre[j] - target]`. Do not forget the empty prefix (value 0) at the very start.

## Hint
Start the dict as {0: 1}. For each day: update the running total, add `count.get(total - target, 0)` to the answer, then record the total in the dict.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `count_exact_streaks`. It has two parameters:
- `changes`, a list of `n` ints (can be negative or zero).
- `target`, an int.

It must return an int: the number of pairs `(i, j)` with `0 <= i <= j < n` such that `changes[i] + ... + changes[j] == target`.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: count_exact_streaks([1, 2, 3, 0, 3], 3) => 5
Example 2: count_exact_streaks([1, -1, 1, -1], 0) => 4
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 15,000
- |changes[i]| <= 10^6
- |target| <= 10^9

## Scoring
- You get 30 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 10.
- You get 50 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 1,500.
- You get 120 points if you solve all test cases.
- Your score is the best tier you fully solve.

problems.title: Gift Card Pairs
problems.statement:
### C1 - Gift Card Pairs

You won a mall gift card with exactly `target` pesos on it, and you do not want to waste a single centavo. You plan to buy TWO different items whose prices add up to exactly `target`.

The mall lists `n` items with their prices. How many different pairs of items (by position in the list) have prices that sum to `target`?

## Algorithm Corner
A dict (hash map) gives you 'have I seen this before?' and 'how many times?' in O(1) on average, which turns many nested loops into one loop.

Looping over all pairs is O(n^2). Instead, loop once. For each price `p`, the partner you need is `target - p`. Ask the dict how many earlier items have exactly that price, add it to the answer, and then record `p` in the dict.

## Hint
Count pairs i < j. When you stand at item j, you only need to look at the items before it, which are already in your dict.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `count_pairs_with_sum`. It has two parameters:
- `prices`, a list of `n` ints.
- `target`, an int.

It must return an int: the number of pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `prices[i] + prices[j] == target`.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: count_pairs_with_sum([1, 5, 3, 3, 3], 6) => 4
Example 2: count_pairs_with_sum([2, 2, 2], 4) => 3
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 15,000
- 1 <= prices[i] <= 10^9
- 1 <= target <= 2 * 10^9

## Scoring

problems.title: Group Chat Anagrams
problems.statement:
### C2 - Group Chat Anagrams

Your org's group chat is full of one-word messages. Two messages are 'twins' if one can be rearranged into the other using exactly the same letters, like `listen` and `silent`.

Given every message in order, how many pairs of messages (by position, i < j) are twins? Identical words are twins too.

## Hint
What do all words in a twin family have in common once you sort their letters? Use that 'signature' as a dict key and count how many words share each signature. A family of c words has c * (c - 1) / 2 pairs.

## Task Details

It must return an int: the number of pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j` such that `words[i]` and `words[j]` are anagrams of each other.

problems.title: Ube-Keso Balance
problems.statement:
### C3 - Ube-Keso Balance

A dirty-ice-cream vendor stacks scoops in a long tray, left to right. Each scoop is either ube (`U`) or keso (`K`).

A customer wants a 'balanced cup': a contiguous stretch of scoops with exactly as many `U` as `K`. What is the length of the longest balanced stretch in the tray? (Return 0 if none exists.)

## Hint
Turn every `U` into +1 and every `K` into -1, and keep a running balance. A stretch is balanced exactly when the balance is the same at its two ends. For each balance value, remember only the FIRST position you saw it (a dict), since the earliest start makes the longest stretch.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `longest_balanced`. Its only parameter is `scoops`, a string of `U` and `K` characters (possibly empty).

It must return an int: the length of the longest contiguous substring with equally many `U` and `K`, or 0 if there is none.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: longest_balanced('UUKKUK') => 6
Example 2: longest_balanced('UUU') => 0
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= length <= 15,000
- the string only contains `U` and `K`

problems.title: Cutoff Grades
problems.statement:
### D1 - Cutoff Grades

The registrar has the exam scores of everyone in the class, already sorted from lowest to highest. Students keep asking: 'If the cutoff is x, how many people got at least x?'

The registrar wants to answer every question without re-reading the whole list each time.

## Algorithm Corner
Binary search finds a position in a SORTED list in O(log n) by repeatedly cutting the search range in half: look at the middle; if it is too small, throw away the left half, otherwise throw away the right half.

A very useful form is 'lower bound': the FIRST index whose value is >= x.

lo, hi = 0, len(a)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] < x:
        lo = mid + 1      # mid is too small, answer is to the right
    else:
        hi = mid          # mid might be the answer, keep it
# lo is now the first index with a[lo] >= x (or len(a))

Everything at index lo and beyond is >= x.

## Hint
The answer for a query x is `len(scores) - lower_bound(x)`. Write the loop above yourself (imports are not allowed).

## Task Details
Implement a function called `count_at_least`. It has two parameters:
- `scores`, a list of `n` ints sorted in non-decreasing order.
- `queries`, a list of `q` ints.

It must return a list of `q` ints: for each query `x`, how many entries of `scores` are `>= x`.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed (write your own binary search).
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: count_at_least([50, 60, 60, 75, 90], [60, 100, 0, 76]) => [4, 0, 5, 1]
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n, q <= 15,000
- 0 <= scores[i] <= 10^6
- -10 <= x <= 10^6 + 10

## Scoring
- You get 30 points if you solve all test cases where n, q <= 10.
- You get 50 points if you solve all test cases where n, q <= 1,500.
- You get 80 points if you solve all test cases.
- Your score is the best tier you fully solve.

problems.title: Nearest Ukay Store

Ukay-ukay stores are scattered along Commonwealth Avenue (a number line). You are walking and, at various positions `x`, you wonder: 'Which store is closest to me?' You can walk in either direction.

If two stores are equally close, you prefer the one with the smaller position. Stores are NOT given in any particular order.

## Hint

problems.title: Sampaguita Garlands
problems.statement:
### D3 - Sampaguita Garlands

Before the Flores de Mayo, you have `n` strips of ribbon of various lengths, and you need to make at least `k` garlands. Every garland must have the SAME whole-number length `L`, and each garland is cut from a single strip (you cannot tie strips together; leftovers are thrown away).

What is the largest length `L` you can use? If you cannot even make `k` garlands of length 1, the answer is 0.

## Algorithm Corner
Binary search on the answer. You do not need a sorted array: you only need a yes/no question that is MONOTONE. Here: 'can I cut at least k pieces of length L?'. If it is yes for some L, it is also yes for any smaller L. So the answers look like YES YES YES ... YES NO NO ... NO, and you binary search for the last YES.

Checking one L costs O(n): a strip of length x gives `x // L` pieces. Total time: O(n log(max length)).

lo, hi = 1, max_length
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2     # round UP when you write lo = mid
    if can_cut(mid): lo = mid
    else: hi = mid - 1

## Hint
First handle the impossible case (even L = 1 fails, meaning the total length is less than k). Then binary search L between 1 and the longest strip.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `max_piece_length`. It has two parameters:
- `ribbons`, a list of `n` positive ints.
- `k`, a positive int.

It must return an int: the largest `L >= 1` such that `sum(x // L for x in ribbons) >= k`, or 0 if no such `L` exists.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: max_piece_length([9, 7, 5], 5) => 3
Example 2: max_piece_length([3, 4], 100) => 0
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 15,000
- 1 <= ribbons[i] <= 10^9
- 1 <= k <= 10^13

## Scoring
- You get 30 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 6 and ribbons[i] <= 30.
- You get 50 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 1,500 and ribbons[i] <= 2,000.
- You get 120 points if you solve all test cases.
- Your score is the best tier you fully solve.

problems.title: Bangka Crossing
problems.statement:
### E1 - Bangka Crossing

A fleet of small bangka (outrigger boats) ferries people across a lake. Every bangka can carry AT MOST TWO people, and the total weight of the people in it must not exceed `limit`. Everyone weighs at most `limit`, so anyone can ride alone.

Given the weights of all the people waiting, what is the minimum number of boats needed to carry everybody across?

## Algorithm Corner
Two pointers: keep one index at each end of a SORTED array and move them toward each other. Here, look at the lightest and the heaviest remaining person. The heaviest person must take a boat anyway. If the lightest can share it, great, let them. If even the lightest cannot fit, nobody can, so the heaviest rides alone.

Each step retires one boat and moves at least one pointer, so the whole thing is O(n) after sorting.

## Hint
Sort the weights. Use `i` for the lightest and `j` for the heaviest. Each iteration uses one boat for person `j`; also advance `i` if `weights[i] + weights[j] <= limit`. Careful when `i == j`: that is a single person.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `min_boats`. It has two parameters:
- `weights`, a list of `n` ints with `1 <= weights[i] <= limit`.
- `limit`, an int.

It must return an int: the minimum number of boats, each carrying at most 2 people with total weight at most `limit`.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: min_boats([3, 2, 2, 1], 3) => 3
Example 2: min_boats([5, 5, 5], 9) => 3
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 15,000
- 1 <= limit <= 10^9
- 1 <= weights[i] <= limit

## Scoring
- You get 30 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 9.
- You get 50 points if you solve all test cases where n <= 1,500.
- You get 80 points if you solve all test cases.
- Your score is the best tier you fully solve.

problems.title: Finals Week Grind
problems.statement:
### E2 - Finals Week Grind

Finals week is coming! On each day you record how many hours you studied (always at least 1 hour per day, you are no slacker).

You want to know the SHORTEST stretch of consecutive days in which you studied a total of at least `target` hours. How many days long is that shortest stretch? If no stretch ever reaches `target`, answer 0.

## Algorithm Corner
A sliding window keeps two indices, `left` and `right`, and a running sum of what is between them. Expand `right` one day at a time. While the window is 'good enough', record its length, then shrink from the left to see if a shorter window is still good.

This works here because every value is POSITIVE: expanding always increases the sum, shrinking always decreases it. Each index moves forward only, so the total work is O(n) even though there are two nested-looking loops.

## Hint
For each new `right`, add `hours[right]` to the sum. While `sum >= target`, update the best length and then subtract `hours[left]` and move `left` forward.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `shortest_grind`. It has two parameters:
- `hours`, a list of `n` positive ints.
- `target`, a positive int.

It must return an int: the length of the shortest contiguous stretch with sum at least `target`, or 0 if there is none.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: shortest_grind([2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3], 7) => 2
Example 2: shortest_grind([1, 1, 1], 10) => 0
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 15,000
- 1 <= hours[i] <= 1,000
- 1 <= target <= 10^8

## Scoring

problems.title: Bracket Bandit
problems.statement:
### F1 - Bracket Bandit

You are writing the syntax checker for a tiny programming language. The only thing it checks is brackets: every opening bracket `(`, `[`, `{` must be closed by the matching closing bracket `)`, `]`, `}` in the correct order, like Russian dolls: the most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed.

`([]{})` is fine. `([)]` is not. `((` is not (never closed). `)(` is not either.

## Algorithm Corner
A stack is 'last in, first out': the thing you pushed most recently is the first thing you pop. That is exactly the shape of nested brackets.

Scan left to right. On an opening bracket, push it. On a closing bracket, the top of the stack MUST be its matching opener: pop it; if the stack is empty or the top does not match, the string is invalid. At the end the stack must be empty (nothing left open).

In Python a list works as a stack: `append` pushes, `pop()` pops the last element.

## Hint
Use a dict like {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'} to find the matching opener. Do not forget both failure cases: wrong match AND leftovers at the end.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `brackets_ok`. Its only parameter is `code`, a string consisting only of the characters `()[]{}` (possibly empty).

It must return a bool: `True` if the brackets are correctly matched and nested, otherwise `False`.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: brackets_ok('([]{})') => True
Example 2: brackets_ok('([)]') => False
Example 3: brackets_ok('((') => False
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= length <= 100,000
- the string only contains `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`

problems.title: Init ng Maynila
problems.statement:
### F2 - Init ng Maynila

It is another scorching summer in Manila. For each day, you wonder: 'How many days do I have to wait until a WARMER day (strictly higher temperature) arrives?'

Given the temperature of every day, answer this for every day. If no warmer day ever comes, the answer for that day is 0.

## Algorithm Corner
A monotonic stack keeps its contents in sorted order (here: temperatures that are still waiting for something warmer, from coldest at the top... well, from warmest at the bottom to the coldest at the top). When a new day arrives, every waiting day that is colder than today has just found its answer, so pop them one by one and fill in their waiting time. Then push today.

Each day is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total work is O(n), even though the double loop looks scary. Store INDICES on the stack so you can compute the waiting time.

## Hint
Loop over days `i`. While the stack is non-empty and `temps[stack[-1]] < temps[i]`, pop `j` and set `answer[j] = i - j`. Then push `i`.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `days_until_warmer`. Its only parameter is `temps`, a list of `n` ints.

It must return a list of `n` ints: for each day `i`, the smallest `d > 0` such that `temps[i + d] > temps[i]`, or 0 if there is no such day.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: days_until_warmer([30, 25, 28, 35, 20, 21, 40]) => [3, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1, 0]
Example 2: days_until_warmer([5, 4, 3]) => [0, 0, 0]
```

## Constraints

- 1 <= temps[i] <= 15,000

problems.title: Billboard Rush
problems.statement:
### F3 - Billboard Rush

Along EDSA there is a row of `n` buildings, each exactly 1 meter wide, with heights `heights[i]` meters. An advertising company wants to hang one rectangular billboard on the skyline. The billboard must sit on the ground and fit completely inside a stretch of CONSECUTIVE buildings (it cannot stick out above any building it covers).

What is the largest billboard area possible?

## Algorithm Corner
This is the famous 'largest rectangle in a histogram'. Brute force tries every stretch and uses its shortest building as the billboard height: O(n^2).

With a stack you do better. Keep the stack of buildings whose heights are INCREASING from bottom to top; each is still 'free to extend to the right'. When a new building is shorter than the top, the top building's billboard can extend no further: pop it and compute its best rectangle (its height times how far left it reaches to how far right it reached). Add a height-0 sentinel at the end to flush everything.

## Hint
When you pop a building of height h, its rectangle spans from the position where it could first start (remember the start index of the popped entry) up to the current index. Push the NEW building with that earliest start index so it can extend leftward.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `largest_billboard`. Its only parameter is `heights`, a list of `n` non-negative ints.

It must return an int: the maximum area of a rectangle covering consecutive buildings, where the rectangle's height is at most the height of every building it covers.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: largest_billboard([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]) => 10
Example 2: largest_billboard([4, 4, 4]) => 12
```

- 0 <= heights[i] <= 10^6

problems.title: Hagdan ng Oble
problems.statement:
### G1 - Hagdan ng Oble

Every year, a freshman climbs the long stairs of the Quezon Hall for photos with the Oblation. The stairs have `n` steps. In one move, a person can climb 1, 2, or 3 steps.

In how many different ways can someone climb exactly `n` steps (order of the moves matters)? Staying at the bottom counts as exactly one way to climb 0 steps. Since the answer can be huge, output it modulo 1,000,000,007.

## Algorithm Corner
Dynamic programming (DP) solves a big problem by combining answers to smaller, overlapping versions of the same problem, and each smaller answer is computed only ONCE.

Define `ways(n)`: the number of ways to climb n steps. Look at the LAST move: it was 1, 2 or 3 steps, so
    ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) + ways(n-3)      with ways(0) = 1
A naive recursion recomputes the same values exponentially many times. Instead, compute ways(0), ways(1), ways(2), ... in order, keeping only the last three values. That is O(n) time and O(1) memory.

## Hint
Start from ways(0) = 1 and treat negative arguments as 0 ways. Take `% 1_000_000_007` inside the loop so numbers stay small. A recursive solution without a cache will be far too slow for big `n`.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `stair_ways`. Its only parameter is `n`, an int with `n >= 0`.

It must return an int: the number of sequences of moves (each 1, 2 or 3) with total exactly `n`, modulo 1,000,000,007.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: stair_ways(4) => 7
Example 2: stair_ways(3) => 4
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 10^6

## Scoring

You may skip any houses. What is the maximum total candy you can collect?

## Hint

problems.title: Ukay-Ukay Backpack
problems.statement:
### G3 - Ukay-Ukay Backpack

It is bargain-hunting day at the ukay-ukay! Your backpack can hold at most `capacity` kilograms. Each item on the rack has a weight and a resale value. You can take each item at most once, and you want the largest possible TOTAL resale value without breaking the backpack.

(This is the legendary 0/1 knapsack problem. Greedy 'best value per kilo first' can fail, so be careful!)

## Algorithm Corner
0/1 knapsack DP: let `dp[c]` be the best total value achievable with a backpack of capacity c using the items processed so far. Process items one at a time. For an item with weight w and value v, every capacity c >= w may improve:
    dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w] + v)
IMPORTANT: loop c from HIGH to LOW. Going downward guarantees `dp[c - w]` still refers to the situation BEFORE this item, so the item is used at most once. (Going upward would let you reuse it, which is the 'unbounded' knapsack.)

Time O(n * capacity).

## Hint
Start with `dp = [0] * (capacity + 1)`. For every item, loop `c` from `capacity` down to `w`. The answer is `dp[capacity]` (since dp is non-decreasing in c).

## Task Details
Implement a function called `best_haul`. It has two parameters:
- `capacity`, an int.
- `items`, a list of `n` pairs `[weight, value]` of positive ints.

It must return an int: the maximum total value of a subset of items whose total weight is at most `capacity`.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: best_haul(10, [[5, 10], [4, 40], [6, 30], [3, 50]]) => 90
Example 2: best_haul(4, [[5, 100]]) => 0
```

## Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 150
- 0 <= capacity <= 5,000
- 1 <= weight <= 200
- 1 <= value <= 10^6

problems.title: Toll Gate Trek
problems.statement:
### H1 - Toll Gate Trek

Going home from UP to the province means crossing a grid-like network of toll gates. `grid[i][j]` is the toll you pay when you pass through the gate at row `i`, column `j`. You start at the top-left gate and must reach the bottom-right gate, and you can only move RIGHT or DOWN one gate at a time. You pay the toll of every gate you pass, including the first and the last.

What is the minimum total toll?

## Algorithm Corner
Grid DP: let `dp[i][j]` be the answer for reaching cell (i, j). Because you can only arrive from the cell above or the cell to the left,
    dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
Fill the table row by row, so that the two cells you depend on are always ready. The first row and first column have only one possible predecessor.

Time O(rows * cols), instead of the exponentially many paths a brute force would try.

## Hint
Handle the corner (0,0) separately: dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]. For the first row, you can only come from the left; for the first column, only from above.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `min_toll`. Its only parameter is `grid`, a list of `r` lists, each with `c` ints (`r, c >= 1`).

It must return an int: the minimum sum of `grid` values along a path from `(0, 0)` to `(r-1, c-1)` moving only right or down.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: min_toll([[1, 3, 1], [1, 5, 1], [4, 2, 1]]) => 7
Example 2: min_toll([[7]]) => 7
```

## Constraints

- 0 <= grid[i][j] <= 100

problems.title: Baha sa Maynila

problems.title: Barkada Circles
problems.statement:
### I1 - Barkada Circles

The freshmen batch has `n` students, numbered 0 to `n-1`. You are given pairs of students who are friends. Friendship is contagious in a barkada: if A is friends with B and B is friends with C, then A, B and C are all in the SAME circle, even if A and C never met.

How many separate friend circles does the batch have? (A student with no friends is a circle of one.)

## Algorithm Corner
A graph has nodes (students) and edges (friend pairs). A 'connected component' is a maximal group of nodes that can reach each other. Counting components is the classic job for UNION-FIND (disjoint set union):

- Every node starts in its own set, so there are n sets.
- `find(x)` follows parent links to the set's representative. Shorten long chains by 'path compression' (point a node closer to the root as you walk).
- For each edge (a, b): if `find(a) != find(b)`, merge the two sets and decrease the set count by 1.

The final count is the number of components. Almost O(n + m) in practice. (BFS/DFS also works: just be careful with recursion depth on 15,000 chained students.)

## Hint
Use a parent list `p = list(range(n))`. A loop `while p[x] != x: p[x] = p[p[x]]; x = p[x]` is an iterative `find` with path halving.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `friend_circles`. It has two parameters:
- `n`, the number of students (`n >= 1`).
- `pairs`, a list of `m` pairs `[a, b]` with `0 <= a, b < n` and `a != b` (a pair may appear more than once).

It must return an int: the number of connected components.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```

Example 2: friend_circles(4, []) => 4
```

## Constraints

- 0 <= m <= 15,000

problems.title: Takas sa Maze
problems.statement:
### I2 - Takas sa Maze

You are lost in the maze of the UP Lagoon garden! The maze is a grid with walls (`#`) and open paths (`.`). You are at `S` and the exit is `E`. In one step you may move to a neighbouring open cell directly UP, DOWN, LEFT or RIGHT (no diagonals), never through a wall.

What is the smallest number of steps needed to reach the exit? If it is impossible, answer -1.

## Algorithm Corner
Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores a graph in 'rings': first the start, then everything 1 step away, then everything 2 steps away, and so on. So the FIRST time BFS reaches a cell, it has used the minimum number of steps (when every move costs the same).

Implementation: a queue (use `collections.deque`, but imports are not allowed here, so a list with a moving head index works too) and a `dist` table. Pop a cell, look at its 4 neighbours, and for every unvisited open neighbour set `dist = dist[current] + 1` and push it. A cell is marked visited the moment it is PUSHED, so it is never queued twice.

## Hint
Find `S` and `E` first by scanning the grid. Use a list as a queue with an index `head` that moves forward instead of `pop(0)` (which is O(n)). Return -1 if the queue runs dry before you reach `E`.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `maze_steps`. Its only parameter is `grid`, a list of `r` strings of length `c` containing exactly one `S`, exactly one `E`, and otherwise `.` and `#`.

It must return an int: the minimum number of steps from `S` to `E` moving in the 4 directions through non-wall cells, or -1 if `E` cannot be reached.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: maze_steps(['S.#', '.#.', '..E']) => 4
Example 2: maze_steps(['S#E']) => -1
```

## Constraints
- 1 <= r, c <= 200
- 2 <= r * c

problems.title: Jeepney Routes
problems.statement:
### I3 - Jeepney Routes

The city has `n` jeepney stops, numbered 1 to `n`. Between some pairs of stops there is a two-way road, and driving along it takes a certain number of minutes (different roads take different times). You are at stop `start` and want to get to stop `end` as quickly as possible, possibly passing through other stops on the way.

What is the shortest possible travel time? If `end` cannot be reached at all, answer -1.

## Algorithm Corner
When roads have different lengths, BFS is no longer enough. Dijkstra's algorithm fixes this: always expand the stop that currently has the SMALLEST known travel time. Since all times are positive, once a stop is the smallest in the queue, nothing can ever improve it.

A priority queue (min-heap) gives you 'the smallest known time' in O(log n). Push `(time, stop)` pairs; when you pop a pair that is already worse than the best known time for that stop, skip it (it is stale). Otherwise relax every outgoing road: if `time + w` beats the known time of the neighbour, update it and push.

Time: O((n + m) log n).

## Hint
Build an adjacency list first: `adj[u]` holds `(v, w)` for every road touching u (add it in both directions!). Keep `dist` as a list with a huge value for 'unknown'.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `fastest_route`. It has four parameters:
- `n`, the number of stops.
- `roads`, a list of `m` triples `[a, b, w]` meaning a two-way road between stops `a` and `b` taking `w` minutes (`1 <= w`). Several roads between the same pair can exist.
- `start` and `end`, two stops (they can be equal).

It must return an int: the minimum total travel time, or -1 if `end` is unreachable from `start`.

## Restrictions
- The following imports are allowed: `heappush` and `heappop` from `heapq`.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: fastest_route(4, [[1, 2, 5], [2, 4, 5], [1, 3, 2], [3, 4, 20]], 1, 4) => 10
Example 2: fastest_route(3, [[1, 2, 1]], 1, 3) => -1
```

## Constraints

- 0 <= m <= 12,000
- 1 <= w <= 10^6

problems.title: Prime Raffle
problems.statement:
### J1 - Prime Raffle

A raffle sells tickets numbered 1, 2, 3, ... and ONLY tickets with a PRIME number can win (the organizer loves primes). Participants keep asking: 'If tickets only go up to q, how many winning tickets are there?'

For each query `q`, count the prime numbers between 1 and `q`, inclusive.

## Algorithm Corner
The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds ALL primes up to a limit M at once in about O(M log log M):

1. Make a list `is_prime` of size M + 1, all True (except 0 and 1).
2. For i = 2, 3, ...: if `is_prime[i]` is still True, it is prime; cross out all its multiples starting at i * i (smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes).
3. You only need to loop i while i * i <= M.

Then a PREFIX SUM over the sieve gives 'number of primes <= q' for every q in O(1). Never test each number separately (trial division per query is far too slow). Sieve once up to the biggest query.

## Hint
Compute the largest query, sieve up to that, build `prime_count[q]` as a running total, then answer every query by lookup.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `count_primes`. Its only parameter is `queries`, a list of `q` ints.

It must return a list of `q` ints: for each query `x`, the number of primes `p` with `p <= x`.

## Restrictions
- No imports are allowed.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```

```

## Constraints

problems.title: Blinking Parols
problems.statement:
### J2 - Blinking Parols

It is Christmas season and a street is decorated with `n` parols (lanterns). The i-th parol blinks every `periods[i]` seconds: it blinks at time 0, at `periods[i]`, at `2 * periods[i]`, and so on. At time 0 ALL parols blink together.

When is the next time (after time 0) that all parols blink at the very same moment?

## Algorithm Corner
The moment parol i blinks are the multiples of its period. A time where ALL blink together is a COMMON MULTIPLE of all periods, and the first one is the LEAST common multiple (LCM).

gcd(a, b) is the greatest common divisor (Euclid: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)`, ending at `gcd(a, 0) = a`), and
    lcm(a, b) = a // gcd(a, b) * b
(divide first to keep numbers smaller). To get the LCM of a whole list, fold it: lcm(lcm(p0, p1), p2), ...

Looping time = 1, 2, 3, ... until everything divides it is far too slow when the answer is huge.

## Hint
Write your own gcd with a `while b:` loop, or use `gcd` from `math` (the only import allowed). Python ints never overflow, so large answers are fine.

## Task Details
Implement a function called `next_sync`. Its only parameter is `periods`, a non-empty list of `n` positive ints.

It must return an int: the smallest `t >= 1` such that `t` is divisible by every period. It is guaranteed that the answer is at most 10^18.

## Restrictions
- The following import is allowed: `gcd` from `math`.
- The source code limit is 2000.

## Example Calls
```
Example 1: next_sync([4, 6]) => 12
Example 2: next_sync([3, 5, 7]) => 105
```

## Constraints
- 1 <= n <= 15,000
- 1 <= periods[i] <= 10^6
- the answer is at most 10^18

problems.title: Kabute Farm
problems.statement:
### J3 - Kabute Farm

You started a mushroom farm. The number of mushrooms on day `n` is described as follows: on days 0, 1, 2, 3 there are 1, 1, 2, 3 mushrooms. From day 4 onward, the count is

    mushrooms(n) = mushrooms(n-1) + mushrooms(n-2) + mushrooms(n-4)

(yesterday's mushrooms stay, the colony from two days ago splits, and the colony from four days ago matures and doubles).

How many mushrooms are there on day `n`? The farm lasts for a very, very long time, so `n` can be up to 10^18. Output the answer modulo 1,000,000,007.

## Algorithm Corner
Looping day by day costs O(n), impossible for n = 10^18. But a linear recurrence can be written as a MATRIX multiplication: keep a state vector of the last four values, and one day is 'multiply by a fixed 4x4 matrix M':

[f(n)  ]   [1 1 0 1] [f(n-1)]
[f(n-1)] = [1 0 0 0] [f(n-2)]
[f(n-2)]   [0 1 0 0] [f(n-3)]
[f(n-3)]   [0 0 1 0] [f(n-4)]

So f(n) comes from M raised to a power, applied to the starting vector. And a power can be computed with FAST EXPONENTIATION (repeated squaring): to compute M^p, square M repeatedly and multiply into the result for each 1-bit of p. That is only about 60 matrix multiplications for p ~ 10^18.

result = identity
while p:
    if p & 1: result = result * M
    M = M * M
    p >>= 1

## Hint
Reduce modulo 1,000,000,007 after every multiplication. Handle n < 4 directly. For n >= 3, the state vector at day 3 is [f(3), f(2), f(1), f(0)] = [3, 2, 1, 1] and you need M^(n-3) applied to it.
